newsitem.title: USA: Japan may be slow to buy more U.S. pork - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Japan may be slow to buy more U.S. pork - analysts.

text.p: U.S. farmers expecting an immediate jump in pork sales to Japan to fill the void left by Taiwan's suspension of pork shipments may be disappointed.

Market analysts and meat processors said the Japanese may not be quick to buy U.S. pork because they have ample supplies in freezers and the foot-and-mouth outbreak in Taiwan may heighten fears about tainted food.
"I think the immediate reaction is to be very cautious about consuming pork at all," said Chris Hurt, agricultural economist at Purdue University, referring to food safety.
"I think that the impact is relatively short term," Hurt said of Japanese consumers' possible concerns about pork.

Although not harmful to humans, the foot-and-mouth outbreak follows an E.Coli outbreak last year that killed 11 people in Japan and sickened 9,000 more. In addition global concerns about Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease being transmitted to humans curbed beef consumption in Japan.
Hurt said the E.Coli outbreak was never officially linked to a particular food, but it "did substantially cut our exports of beef to Japan late last year."
Beef and pork processor Excel Corp., a unit of Cargill Inc, said Japanese buyers began calling about pork purchases soon after Taiwan announced the pork export ban last week.
"We've had increased interest from the Japanese (for pork) but no real significant transactions," said Cargill spokesman Mark Klein.

Klein said pork sales to Japan may be slow to develop because of ample supplies in freezers there. Also, higher pork prices here after Taiwan announced the ban may discourage the Japanese from buying soon.
A spokesman for IBP Inc last week also said it had received increased interest in its pork products from Japan after news of the Taiwan pork ban.
Excel's Klein said the Japanese have not yet expressed interest in buying more U.S. beef but some analysts said they may.

"With U.S. hog supplies extremely tight, Japan may turn to (U.S.) beef supplies, which should be plentiful through the summer," said John McMillin, a food company analyst with Prudential Securities. "We think this Taiwan pork situation has the potential to help the beef export situation to Japan."
Citing Japan's Ministry of Finance figures, the U.S. Meat Export Federation said Taiwan in 1996 shipped 266,225 tonnes of pork to Japan versus 141,790 tonnes from the U.S.
Ron Plain, agricultural economist at the University of Missouri, estimates the U.S. pork industry may pick up about two-thirds of Taiwan's market share to Japan during the next 18 months.

This increase in pork exports may add $5 per cwt to the average U.S. hog price during the 18 months, he said. After that, the U.S. hog industry will have expanded, which should drive hog prices lower.
Plain said he doubts the foot-and-mouth outbreak will hurt pork consumption in Japan, nor does he believe there will be an increase in beef exports.
"Foot and mouth is not a threat to people, it's only a threat to animals," he said.
